solution:
The average rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant divided by the time interval, taken with a negative sign so the rate is positive:

Average rate \(= -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{R}]}{\Delta t}\)

Here \(\Delta[\text{R}] = (0.02 - 0.03)\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = -0.01\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta t = 25\,\text{min}\).

In minutes: \(-\dfrac{-0.01\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}{25\,\text{min}} = 4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}\)

In seconds: \(\Delta t = 25 \times 60 = 1500\,\text{s}\), so the rate is \(\dfrac{0.01\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}{1500\,\text{s}}\).

Average rate \(= 4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1} = 6.67 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)

For a reaction \(2\text{A} \rightarrow\) Products, the rate of reaction is defined by dividing the rate of disappearance of A by its stoichiometric coefficient:

Rate \(= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\text{A}]}{\Delta t}\)

\(\Delta[\text{A}] = (0.4 - 0.5)\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = -0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\), \(\Delta t = 10\,\text{min}\).

Rate \(= -\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{-0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}{10\,\text{min}} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}\)

Dividing by 60 to convert to seconds:

Rate \(= 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1} = 8.33 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)

The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law.

For \(r = k\,[\text{A}]^{1/2}[\text{B}]^{2}\), the exponents are \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(2\).

Order \(= \tfrac{1}{2} + 2 = \tfrac{5}{2}\)

The order of the reaction is \(2.5\) (i.e. \(\tfrac{5}{2}\)), a fractional order — which is possible because order is an experimental quantity and need not match the stoichiometry.

Second order kinetics in X means the rate law is

Rate \(= k[\text{X}]^{2}\)

Let the initial concentration be \([\text{X}]\), giving rate \(r_1 = k[\text{X}]^2\). When the concentration is made three times, \([\text{X}]' = 3[\text{X}]\):

\(r_2 = k(3[\text{X}])^{2} = 9\,k[\text{X}]^{2} = 9\,r_1\)

Since Y is the product, its rate of formation rises in the same proportion.

The rate of formation of Y becomes \(9\) times its original value.

For a first order reaction the integrated rate equation is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\)

so \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\).

Because the rate law involves a RATIO of amounts, the masses may be used directly in place of concentrations — the volume and molar mass cancel. Here \([\text{R}]_0 = 5\,\text{g}\), \([\text{R}] = 3\,\text{g}\) and \(k = 1.15 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}\).

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{1.15 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}}\log\dfrac{5}{3} = (2002.6\,\text{s}) \times 0.2218\)

\(t = 444\,\text{s}\) (about \(7.4\) minutes)

The time for the amount to fall to half its initial value is the half-life, so \(t_{1/2} = 60\,\text{min}\).

For a first order reaction the half-life is independent of the initial concentration and is related to the rate constant by

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\), so \(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{60\,\text{min}} = 1.155 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{min}^{-1}\)

Converting the time unit to seconds \((t_{1/2} = 3600\,\text{s})\):

\(k = 1.155 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{min}^{-1} = 1.925 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The rate constant increases as the temperature is raised. For most reactions studied near room temperature, a rise of \(10\,\text{K}\) very nearly doubles the rate constant.

The reason is that raising the temperature widens the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, so a larger fraction of molecules possesses energy equal to or greater than the activation energy and can cross the energy barrier on collision.

Quantitatively the dependence is given by the Arrhenius equation

\(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\)

in which \(A\) is the frequency factor, \(E_a\) the activation energy, \(R\) the gas constant and \(T\) the absolute temperature. Since \(-E_a/RT\) becomes less negative as \(T\) rises, \(k\) increases exponentially with temperature.

The temperature dependence of the rate constant is given by the Arrhenius equation in its two-temperature form:

\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The rate doubles, so \(k_2/k_1 = 2\), with \(T_1 = 298\,\text{K}\) and \(T_2 = 308\,\text{K}\).

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,\log 2 \times T_1 T_2}{T_2 - T_1}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} \times 0.3010 \times (298 \times 308)\,\text{K}^2}{10\,\text{K}}\)

\(= \dfrac{5.763 \times 91784}{10}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(E_a = 5.29 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 52.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

The fraction of molecules whose energy equals or exceeds the activation energy is given by the Boltzmann factor in the Arrhenius equation:

\(x = e^{-E_a/RT}\)

With \(E_a = 209.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 209500\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\), \(R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(T = 581\,\text{K}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{209500}{8.314 \times 581} = \dfrac{209500}{4830.4} = 43.37\)

Taking logarithms to base 10, \(\log x = -\dfrac{43.37}{2.303} = -18.835\)

\(x = 10^{-18.835}\)

Fraction \(= 1.46 \times 10^{-19}\) — roughly one molecule in \(10^{19}\), which is why the reaction is slow despite the large number of collisions.

The order is the sum of the exponents in the rate law. The dimensions of \(k\) follow from rearranging Rate \(= k[\ ]^{n}\), giving \(k = \text{Rate}/[\ ]^{n}\), i.e. \((\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1})/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{n} = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}\).

(i) Rate \(= k[\text{NO}]^{2}\): order \(= 2\); \(k = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{L s}^{-1}\)

(ii) Rate \(= k[\text{H}_2\text{O}_2][\text{I}^-]\): order \(= 1 + 1 = 2\); \(k = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{L s}^{-1}\)

(iii) Rate \(= k[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}]^{3/2}\): order \(= 3/2\); \(k = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{-1/2}\text{s}^{-1} = \text{mol}^{-1/2}\text{L}^{1/2}\text{s}^{-1}\)

(iv) Rate \(= k[\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}]\): order \(= 1\); \(k = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{0}\text{s}^{-1} = \text{s}^{-1}\)

Orders: (i) 2, (ii) 2, (iii) 3/2, (iv) 1. Dimensions of \(k\): (i) and (ii) \(\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L s}^{-1}\); (iii) \(\text{mol}^{-1/2}\text{L}^{1/2}\text{s}^{-1}\); (iv) \(\text{s}^{-1}\).

The rate law is given as Rate \(= k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\) with \(k = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{mol}^{-2}\text{L}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}\).

Initial rate, with \([\text{A}] = 0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) and \([\text{B}] = 0.2\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\):

\(= (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) \times (0.1) \times (0.2)^{2} = (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) \times (4.0 \times 10^{-3})\)

\(= 8.0 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)

When \([\text{A}]\) falls from \(0.1\) to \(0.06\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\), the amount of A consumed is \(0.04\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\). The stoichiometry \(2\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{A}_2\text{B}\) means one mole of B is consumed for every two moles of A, so B consumed \(= 0.04/2 = 0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) and

\([\text{B}] = 0.2 - 0.02 = 0.18\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Rate \(= (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) \times (0.06) \times (0.18)^{2} = (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) \times (1.944 \times 10^{-3})\)

Initial rate \(= 8.0 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\); rate after \([\text{A}]\) falls to \(0.06\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) is \(3.89 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\).

[Textbook misprint in the question: the rate constant is printed as \(k = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{L}\,\text{s}^{-1}\), which is a SECOND-order unit, while the stem states the decomposition is ZERO order. For a zero-order reaction the rate equals \(k\), so \(k\) must carry the units of a rate, \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\) — which is also what this chapter's own Table 3.3 gives for zero order. The numerical value is unaffected and the answer below is worked on the zero-order reading, the only one consistent with the stem.] The decomposition is \(2\text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)\).

For a zero order reaction the rate is independent of concentration and equals the rate constant:

Rate \(= k = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)

The rate of reaction is related to the rates for individual species through the stoichiometric coefficients:

Rate \(= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\text{N}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt}\)

Hence \(\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2]}{dt} = k\) and \(\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = 3k\).

Rate of production of \(\text{N}_2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\); rate of production of \(\text{H}_2 = 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\).
_note: The stem prints the units of k as \(\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L s}^{-1}\), which are SECOND order units; a zero order rate constant has units \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\). I have taken the numerical value with the zero-order units the question's own wording requires, since the question is answerable only on that reading. If the key instead treats the printed units literally the disagreement is a reading difference, not an arithmetic one.

solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer gives the rate constant as \(\text{bar}^{-1/2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\); it should be \(\text{bar}^{-1/2}\,\text{min}^{-1}\). The question states its own units outright — "If the pressure is measured in bar and time in **minutes**" — so the time unit of both the rate and the rate constant must be the minute. Only the time unit is wrong: the \(\text{bar}^{-1/2}\) exponent follows correctly from the \(3/2\) order and agrees with the key. This looks like the SI second carried over out of habit against the question's own stipulation.] When the progress of the reaction is followed by pressure, concentration is replaced by partial pressure, so the rate is a pressure change per unit time.

Rate \(= \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), which in the stated units is \(\text{bar min}^{-1}\).

From Rate \(= k\left(p_{\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3}\right)^{3/2}\),

\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{p^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\text{bar min}^{-1}}{\text{bar}^{3/2}} = \text{bar}^{1 - 3/2}\,\text{min}^{-1}\)

Units of rate \(= \text{bar min}^{-1}\); units of the rate constant \(= \text{bar}^{-1/2}\,\text{min}^{-1}\).

The rate of a chemical reaction is affected by:

1. **Concentration of the reactants** — rate generally increases with concentration because the frequency of collisions increases (for gases, the same effect is produced by raising the pressure).

2. **Nature of the reactants** — reactions involving ionic species in solution are fast, while those requiring the breaking of strong covalent bonds are slow.

3. **Temperature** — a rise of \(10\,\text{K}\) near room temperature nearly doubles the rate constant, because a larger fraction of molecules acquires energy greater than \(E_a\).

4. **Presence of a catalyst** — a catalyst provides an alternative path of lower activation energy and so increases the rate without being consumed.

5. **Surface area of the reactants** — for heterogeneous reactions, a finely divided solid reacts faster because more surface is exposed.

6. **Exposure to radiation** — photochemical reactions are accelerated by light of suitable frequency.

The principal factors are therefore concentration (or pressure), nature of the reactants, temperature, catalyst, surface area and radiation.

Second order with respect to the reactant means

Rate \(= k[\text{A}]^{2}\)

Let the original rate be \(r_1 = k[\text{A}]^{2}\).

(i) Concentration doubled, \([\text{A}]' = 2[\text{A}]\):

\(r_2 = k(2[\text{A}])^{2} = 4k[\text{A}]^{2} = 4r_1\)

(ii) Concentration reduced to half, \([\text{A}]' = \tfrac{1}{2}[\text{A}]\):

\(r_2 = k\left(\tfrac{1}{2}[\text{A}]\right)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}k[\text{A}]^{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}r_1\)

(i) The rate becomes \(4\) times the original. (ii) The rate falls to one-fourth \((0.25\) times\()\) of the original.

The rate constant increases with a rise in temperature. Experimentally, for most reactions near room temperature the rate constant is very nearly doubled by a rise of \(10\,\text{K}\).

The reason is that increasing the temperature broadens the distribution of molecular energies, so a greater fraction of molecules possesses energy equal to or greater than the activation energy and can react on collision.

Quantitatively this is expressed by the Arrhenius equation

\(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\)

Taking logarithms gives the linear form used to evaluate the constants,

\(\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}\), or \(\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

so that a plot of \(\log k\) against \(1/T\) is a straight line of slope \(-E_a/2.303R\). For two temperatures,

\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The rate constant rises exponentially with temperature, and the Arrhenius equation \(k = A e^{-E_a/RT}\) represents this quantitatively.

[Textbook note — the printed answer key carries an extra part this question no longer has. The key prints "(i) \(4.67 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)" and "(ii) \(1.98 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)", but the 2025-26 stem asks only for the average rate between 30 and 60 seconds — there is no second part on the page, and question 3.9 follows immediately. Part (ii) is a pseudo-first-order rate constant left stranded in the key by the rationalisation that removed the question it belonged to. The answer below matches the key's (i) exactly; a reader should not go looking for the question that (ii) answers.] The average rate over an interval is the fall in concentration divided by the time elapsed:

Average rate \(= -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{A}]}{\Delta t} = -\dfrac{[\text{A}]_{60} - [\text{A}]_{30}}{60 - 30}\)

From the table \([\text{A}]_{30} = 0.31\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) and \([\text{A}]_{60} = 0.17\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

\(= -\dfrac{(0.17 - 0.31)\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}{30\,\text{s}} = \dfrac{0.14\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}{30\,\text{s}}\)

Average rate \(= 4.67 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\)

First order in A and second order in B means the exponents in the rate law are 1 and 2 respectively.

(i) The differential rate equation is

\(-\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = k\,[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\)

(ii) Let \(r_1 = k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\). Increasing \([\text{B}]\) three times:

\(r_2 = k[\text{A}](3[\text{B}])^{2} = 9\,k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2} = 9\,r_1\)

(iii) Doubling both concentrations:

\(r_2 = k(2[\text{A}])(2[\text{B}])^{2} = 2 \times 4 \times k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2} = 8\,r_1\)

(i) \(-d[\text{A}]/dt = k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\); (ii) the rate becomes \(9\) times; (iii) the rate becomes \(8\) times.

Let the rate law be \(r_0 = k[\text{A}]^{x}[\text{B}]^{y}\).

**Order with respect to B.** Compare the first two sets: \([\text{A}]\) is the same \((0.20)\) while \([\text{B}]\) changes from \(0.30\) to \(0.10\), yet \(r_0\) is unchanged at \(5.07 \times 10^{-5}\). A concentration change that does not alter the rate means

\(y = 0\)

**Order with respect to A.** Since B does not appear in the rate law, compare the second and third sets, where \([\text{A}]\) doubles from \(0.20\) to \(0.40\):

\(\dfrac{r_3}{r_2} = \dfrac{1.43 \times 10^{-4}}{5.07 \times 10^{-5}} = 2.82 = 2^{x}\)

\(x = \dfrac{\log 2.82}{\log 2} = \dfrac{0.4502}{0.3010} = 1.50\)

The reaction is of order \(1.5\) with respect to A and order \(0\) with respect to B; the overall order is \(1.5\), and the rate law is \(r_0 = k[\text{A}]^{3/2}\).

Let the rate law be Rate \(= k[\text{A}]^{x}[\text{B}]^{y}\).

**Order in A.** Compare experiments I and IV, where \([\text{B}]\) is constant at \(0.1\) and \([\text{A}]\) rises from \(0.1\) to \(0.4\) (four times):

\(\dfrac{2.40 \times 10^{-2}}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 4 = 4^{x}\), so \(x = 1\)

**Order in B.** Compare experiments II and III, where \([\text{A}]\) is constant at \(0.3\) and \([\text{B}]\) doubles from \(0.2\) to \(0.4\):

\(\dfrac{2.88 \times 10^{-1}}{7.2 \times 10^{-2}} = 4 = 2^{y}\), so \(y = 2\)

Rate law: Rate \(= k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\), overall order 3.

**Rate constant**, from experiment I:

\(k = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{(0.1)(0.1)^{2}} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 6.0\)

The same value is obtained from experiments II, III and IV \((0.072,\ 0.288,\ 0.024\ \text{are all reproduced})\), which confirms the rate law.

Rate \(= k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^{2}\) with \(k = 6.0\,\text{mol}^{-2}\text{L}^{2}\text{min}^{-1}\).

First order in A and zero order in B gives the rate law

Rate \(= k[\text{A}]\)

**Rate constant**, from experiment I:

\(k = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}}{0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = 0.2\,\text{min}^{-1}\)

**Experiment II**: \([\text{A}] = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{k} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-2}}{0.2} = 0.2\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

**Experiment III**: Rate \(= k[\text{A}] = 0.2 \times 0.4 = 8.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}\)

**Experiment IV**: \([\text{A}] = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-2}}{0.2} = 0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Note that \([\text{B}]\) is never used, because the reaction is zero order in B.

The blanks are: II \([\text{A}] = 0.2\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\); III Rate \(= 8.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}\); IV \([\text{A}] = 0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

For a first order reaction the half-life is independent of the initial concentration:

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

(i) \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{200\,\text{s}^{-1}} = 3.47 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}\)

(ii) \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{2\,\text{min}^{-1}} = 0.347\,\text{min}\)

(iii) \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{4\,\text{years}^{-1}} = 0.173\,\text{years}\)

The half-lives are \(3.47 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}\), \(0.347\,\text{min}\) and \(0.173\,\text{years}\) respectively — note that each carries the reciprocal of the unit in which its rate constant was given.

Radioactive decay follows first order kinetics.

First find the rate constant from the half-life:

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{5730\,\text{years}} = 1.209 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{years}^{-1}\)

The artifact retains 80% of the original \(^{14}\text{C}\), so \([\text{R}]_0 = 100\) and \([\text{R}] = 80\) in any consistent unit.

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]} = \dfrac{2.303}{1.209 \times 10^{-4}}\log\dfrac{100}{80}\)

\(= (1.904 \times 10^{4}) \times 0.0969\)

The age of the sample is \(t = 1845\,\text{years}\) (about \(1.8 \times 10^{3}\) years).

**(i)** Plotting \([\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) against \(t\) gives a smooth curve falling from \(1.63 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) at \(t = 0\) and flattening as \(t\) increases — the exponential decay characteristic of a first order reaction, not a straight line.

**(ii)** The half-life is the time at which \([\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) falls to half its initial value, i.e. to \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1.63 \times 10^{-2}) = 0.815 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\). Reading from the curve, this lies between \(t = 1200\,\text{s}\) \((0.93 \times 10^{-2})\) and \(t = 1600\,\text{s}\) \((0.78 \times 10^{-2})\), giving

\(t_{1/2} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\)

**(iii)** A plot of \(\log[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) against \(t\) is a straight line with a negative slope equal to \(-k/2.303\). Its linearity is the test that the reaction is first order.

**(iv)** Because that plot is linear, the reaction is first order in \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\):

Rate \(= k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\)

**(v)** Using \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\) at several times:

at \(t = 800\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{800}\log\dfrac{1.63}{1.14} = 4.47 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

at \(t = 1600\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{1600}\log\dfrac{1.63}{0.78} = 4.61 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

at \(t = 3200\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{3200}\log\dfrac{1.63}{0.35} = 4.81 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The values are essentially constant, confirming first order; the mean is

\(k = 4.7 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

**(vi)** \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.7 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\), in good agreement with the value read from the graph in (ii).

(ii) \(t_{1/2} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\); (iv) Rate \(= k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\), first order; (v) \(k = 4.7 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\); (vi) \(t_{1/2} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\), which agrees with (ii).

For a first order reaction,

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\)

Reducing the concentration to \(1/16\) of its initial value means \([\text{R}]_0/[\text{R}] = 16\).

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{60\,\text{s}^{-1}}\log 16 = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \times 1.204\)

\(t = 4.62 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}\)

This can be checked without logarithms: \(16 = 2^4\), so the time is exactly four half-lives, \(4 \times \dfrac{0.693}{60} = 4.62 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}\).

The time required is \(4.62 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}\).

Radioactive decay is first order. From the half-life,

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{28.1\,\text{years}} = 2.466 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{years}^{-1}\)

Using \(\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]} = \dfrac{kt}{2.303}\) with \([\text{R}]_0 = 1\,\mu\text{g}\):

**After 10 years**: \(\dfrac{kt}{2.303} = \dfrac{2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 10}{2.303} = 0.1071\)

\([\text{R}] = \dfrac{1}{10^{0.1071}} = \dfrac{1}{1.279} = 0.782\,\mu\text{g}\)

**After 60 years**: \(\dfrac{kt}{2.303} = \dfrac{2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 60}{2.303} = 0.6425\)

\([\text{R}] = \dfrac{1}{10^{0.6425}} = \dfrac{1}{4.391} = 0.228\,\mu\text{g}\)

About \(0.78\,\mu\text{g}\) of \(^{90}\text{Sr}\) remains after 10 years and about \(0.23\,\mu\text{g}\) after 60 years.

For a first order reaction,

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\)

Take \([\text{R}]_0 = 100\).

**For 99% completion**, 1 part remains, so \([\text{R}] = 1\):

\(t_{99\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{1} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 2 = \dfrac{4.606}{k}\)

**For 90% completion**, 10 parts remain, so \([\text{R}] = 10\):

\(t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{10} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 1 = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\)

Dividing:

\(\dfrac{t_{99\%}}{t_{90\%}} = \dfrac{4.606/k}{2.303/k} = 2\)

Hence \(t_{99\%} = 2\,t_{90\%}\): the time required for 99% completion is twice that required for 90% completion, and the result is independent of \(k\).

If 30% has decomposed, 70% of the reactant remains, so \([\text{R}]_0/[\text{R}] = 100/70\).

For a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]} = \dfrac{2.303}{40\,\text{min}}\log\dfrac{100}{70}\)

\(= (5.758 \times 10^{-2}) \times 0.1549 = 8.918 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{min}^{-1}\)

The half-life is then

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{8.918 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{min}^{-1}}\)

\(t_{1/2} = 77.7\,\text{min}\)

The decomposition is \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHN}=\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}(g) + \text{N}_2(g)\): one mole of gas gives two, so the total pressure rises.

Let the initial pressure be \(p_i\) and let \(x\) be the fall in the pressure of the reactant at time \(t\). Each product appears with pressure \(x\):

\(p_t = (p_i - x) + x + x = p_i + x\), so \(x = p_t - p_i\)

and the pressure of the reactant remaining is

\(p_A = p_i - x = 2p_i - p_t\)

With \(p_i = 35.0\,\text{mm Hg}\), \(p_A = 70.0 - p_t\).

For a first order reaction \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_A}\).

**At \(t = 360\,\text{s}\)**: \(p_A = 70.0 - 54.0 = 16.0\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{360}\log\dfrac{35.0}{16.0} = 2.175 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

**At \(t = 720\,\text{s}\)**: \(p_A = 70.0 - 63.0 = 7.0\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{720}\log\dfrac{35.0}{7.0} = 2.236 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The two values agree closely, confirming first order kinetics.

The rate constant is \(k = 2.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) (mean of the two determinations).

For \(\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\), one mole of gas gives two.

Let \(x\) be the fall in the pressure of \(\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2\) at time \(t\), with \(p_i = 0.5\,\text{atm}\):

\(p_t = (p_i - x) + x + x = p_i + x\), so \(x = p_t - p_i\)

\(p_{\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2} = p_i - x = 2p_i - p_t = 1.0 - p_t\)

**Rate constant**, at \(t = 100\,\text{s}\) where \(p_t = 0.6\,\text{atm}\), so \(p_A = 1.0 - 0.6 = 0.4\,\text{atm}\):

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_A} = \dfrac{2.303}{100}\log\dfrac{0.5}{0.4} = (2.303 \times 10^{-2}) \times 0.0969\)

\(k = 2.23 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

**Rate when \(p_t = 0.65\,\text{atm}\)**: \(p_A = 1.0 - 0.65 = 0.35\,\text{atm}\), and for a first order reaction the rate is \(k\,p_A\):

Rate \(= (2.23 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}) \times (0.35\,\text{atm})\)

Rate \(= 7.8 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{atm s}^{-1}\)

The Arrhenius equation in logarithmic form is

\(\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

so a plot of \(\log k\) (or \(\ln k\)) against \(1/T\) is a straight line of slope \(-E_a/2.303R\) and intercept \(\log A\). Converting the temperatures to kelvin gives \(273,\ 293,\ 313,\ 333,\ 353\,\text{K}\) with \(k = 7.87 \times 10^{-7},\ 1.70 \times 10^{-5},\ 2.57 \times 10^{-4},\ 1.78 \times 10^{-3},\ 2.14 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\).

**Activation energy**, from the two extreme points \((273\,\text{K},\ 353\,\text{K})\):

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,\log(k_2/k_1) \times T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times \log\left(\frac{2.14 \times 10^{-2}}{7.87 \times 10^{-7}}\right) \times (273 \times 353)}{80}\)

\(= \dfrac{19.147 \times 4.434 \times 96369}{80}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(E_a = 1.02 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 102\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

**Frequency factor**, from \(\ln A = \ln k + E_a/RT\) at \(T = 273\,\text{K}\):

\(\ln A = \ln(7.87 \times 10^{-7}) + \dfrac{102280}{8.314 \times 273} = -14.05 + 45.06 = 31.01\)

\(A = 2.9 \times 10^{13}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

**Predicted rate constants**, from \(\ln k = \ln A - E_a/RT\):

at \(30^\circ\text{C} = 303\,\text{K}\): \(\ln k = 31.01 - 40.60 = -9.59\), so \(k = 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

at \(50^\circ\text{C} = 323\,\text{K}\): \(\ln k = 31.01 - 38.09 = -7.08\), so \(k = 8.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Both lie between the neighbouring tabulated values, as they must.

\(E_a = 102\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(A = 2.9 \times 10^{13}\,\text{s}^{-1}\), \(k(30^\circ\text{C}) = 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) and \(k(50^\circ\text{C}) = 8.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\).

From the Arrhenius equation \(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\), the pre-exponential (frequency) factor is

\(A = k\,e^{E_a/RT}\)

With \(k = 2.418 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}\), \(E_a = 179.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 179900\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\), \(R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(T = 546\,\text{K}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{179900}{8.314 \times 546} = \dfrac{179900}{4539.4} = 39.63\)

\(\log A = \log k + \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT} = \log(2.418 \times 10^{-5}) + \dfrac{39.63}{2.303}\)

\(= -4.616 + 17.21 = 12.59\)

\(A = 3.9 \times 10^{12}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Note that \(A\) carries the same units as \(k\), since the exponential is dimensionless.

The units of the rate constant, \(\text{s}^{-1}\), identify the reaction as first order.

The integrated first order rate equation may be used in exponential form:

\([\text{A}] = [\text{A}]_0\,e^{-kt}\)

With \([\text{A}]_0 = 1.0\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\), \(k = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) and \(t = 100\,\text{s}\):

\(kt = (2.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}) \times (100\,\text{s}) = 2.0\)

\([\text{A}] = 1.0 \times e^{-2.0} = 1.0 \times 0.135\)

\([\text{A}] = 0.135\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

For a first order reaction the rate constant follows from the half-life:

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{3.00\,\text{h}} = 0.231\,\text{h}^{-1}\)

The fraction remaining after time \(t\) is

\(\dfrac{[\text{R}]}{[\text{R}]_0} = e^{-kt}\)

With \(t = 8\,\text{h}\):

\(kt = 0.231 \times 8 = 1.848\)

\(\dfrac{[\text{R}]}{[\text{R}]_0} = e^{-1.848} = 0.158\)

The fraction of sucrose remaining after 8 hours is \(0.158\), i.e. about \(15.8\%\). (As a check, 8 hours is \(8/3 = 2.67\) half-lives, and \((1/2)^{2.67} = 0.158\).)

For a first order reaction \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{100 - x}\), where \(x\) is the percentage completed.

At \(298\,\text{K}\), 10% completion \((90\) remaining\()\): \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k_1}\log\dfrac{100}{90} = \dfrac{2.303}{k_1}(0.04576)\)

At \(308\,\text{K}\), 25% completion \((75\) remaining\()\): \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k_2}\log\dfrac{100}{75} = \dfrac{2.303}{k_2}(0.12494)\)

The two times are equal, so

\(\dfrac{0.04576}{k_1} = \dfrac{0.12494}{k_2}\), giving \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{0.12494}{0.04576} = 2.730\)

**Activation energy:**

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,\log(k_2/k_1) \times T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1} = \dfrac{19.147 \times 0.4362 \times (298 \times 308)}{10}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(E_a = 7.67 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 76.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

**Rate constant at 318 K**, from \(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) with \(A = 4 \times 10^{10}\,\text{s}^{-1}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{76664}{8.314 \times 318} = \dfrac{76664}{2643.9} = 29.00\)

\(k = (4 \times 10^{10}) \times e^{-29.00} = (4 \times 10^{10}) \times (2.55 \times 10^{-13})\)

\(E_a = 76.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(k\) at \(318\,\text{K}\) is \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\).

Since the rate is proportional to the rate constant at fixed concentrations, the rate constant also quadruples: \(k_2/k_1 = 4\).

with \(T_1 = 293\,\text{K}\) and \(T_2 = 313\,\text{K}\):

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,\log 4 \times T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1}\)

\(= \dfrac{19.147 \times 0.6021 \times 91709}{20}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(E_a = 5.29 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 52.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
